before_taxonomy.classification_basis: Investigators submitted a low-resolution surveillance image to facial recognition, obtained 73 candidates and selected Woodruff as an investigative lead through human narrowing and peer review. A witness then selected her from a separately prepared photo lineup; a captain, prosecutor and magistrate approved the subsequent warrant. The actual arrest was of the wrong person, but these intervening decisions prevent treating the model result as automatic arrest authority. The August 2025 court expressly did not decide whether the facial-recognition lead tainted the witness's later selection; the independent evidentiary validity of that authority basis is therefore unresolved. This materially engages Inferential Evidence–Authority Separation without demonstrating either impermissible promotion of model inference into binding authority or adequate independence of the later coercive decision. The facial-recognition investigative lead received documented peer review, and a separately prepared photo lineup was administered before the warrant. Those verification steps occurred; the later incorrect arrest does not itself establish that a required check was omitted. The court record does not supply a complete contemporaneous methodology for narrowing 73 candidates, nor establish that a particular additional identity or lineup-independence check was mandatory and omitted before a completed verification claim. The court also declined to decide the ACLU's proposed facial-recognition-taint argument. Required Verification Completion is materially engaged at the point where an AI-sourced lead acquired investigative assurance, but the specific required-unperformed-check condition and a positively adequate success-side verification chain remain unestablished. The facial-recognition search returned 73 candidates from a low-definition camera image, investigators narrowed that output to one suspect through peer review, and the witness then selected the same person in a separate lineup. The resulting information reached a high-consequence warrant workflow. The court record does not reconstruct the ranking methodology or establish whether the witness lineup was independent of the machine-generated lead; it also notes the later arrest was of the wrong person. These gaps materially engage the sufficiency of epistemic assurance for consequential reliance, but the warrant was not based on a facial match alone: intervening corroborative processes and judicial approvals were documented. The court found probable cause was not disproven on the submitted claims and left the lineup-taint question undecided. The exact unacceptable-assurance threshold or an affirmatively adequate independent reliance decision is not proven, so no failure or successful-invariant polarity is asserted.
